title: Go SDK: stream backpressure, retry semantics, and ergonomics for long-lived responses
creator: Aisha Patel
description: Goal: Implement robust streaming ergonomics in the Go SDK that: 1) properly propagates context cancellation and deadlines, 2) implements practical backpressure to avoid unbounded memory growth when consumers are slow, and 3) defines clear retry semantics for transient transport errors without violating API semantics for streaming requests. Motivation: production services increasingly rely on long-lived generation streams (chat completions, token-by-token outputs). Current lightweight implementations either buffer entire streams or drop data under pressure; both are unacceptable for reliability and cost. This ticket covers the API shape, runtime primitives, tests, examples, and a migration path for existing users.
acceptance_criteria: - Context cancellation/deadline propagation is honored: WithContext and WithTimeout cancel inflight reads/writes; no goroutine leaks after caller cancels. - Backpressure mechanism prevents unbounded buffering: default client uses a bounded channel + configurable buffer size; docs show how to tune. - When transport errors occur mid-stream, client surfaces a typed error (StreamInterruptedError) with resume not allowed; the library does not automatically retry mid-stream. - For idempotent server-side endpoints that support resumable streams (flagged in model metadata), SDK exposes an opt-in ResumeToken mechanism and example. - Unit and integration tests cover cancellation, slow consumer, and transient network failures. - Benchmarks demonstrate <2% added latency for non-streaming RPCs and provide throughput plots for common buffer sizes. - SDK docs and example repository updated with at least two streaming examples: “chat incremental consumer” and “file export with backpressure”.
design_notes: API surface: add type StreamReader with methods: Recv() (string, error), Close() error, Context() context.Context and a constructor on Client: StartStream(ctx context.Context, req StartStreamRequest, opts ...StreamOption) (*StreamReader, error). Backpressure: internally use a bounded channel of bytes/chunks (default 64 messages) and optional ApplyBackpressure bool; when buffer full we suspend reading from network (via ReadLoop blocking) to rely on HTTP2 flow control; for transports without pushback (SSE), we use an internal read semaphore to drop/slow Read from network layer. Cancellation semantics: StartStream inherits ctx; Recv returns io.EOF when server finishes; if caller cancels ctx, Recv returns context.Canceled and goroutines clean up. Retries: streaming requests are not retried by default. If server declares resume support with a Resume-Token header, we expose ResumeToken on StreamReader and a ResumeFrom(token) helper. Trade-offs: automatic resume complicates guarantees and ordering; opted for opt-in resume only for endpoints that advertise support. Concurrency: Recv is safe for a single consumer goroutine only (documented); we provide a helper adapter that fans-out to multiple consumers with explicit buffering. Error model: introduce StreamInterruptedError (transient network) and StreamCanceledError. Code will avoid global goroutine pools to simplify lifecycle reasoning.

implementation_notes: - Use context.WithCancel propagation and ensure ReadLoop selects on ctx.Done(). - For HTTP/2 transports rely on net/http keep-alive + blocking reads that automatically apply window backpressure; for SSE/websocket add a per-connection semaphore to avoid reading more than buffer capacity. - Implement leak tests that create N streams and cancel; assert goroutine delta <= 3 after 1s. - Add a test server variant that returns a Resume-Token header; validate ResumeFrom(token) resumes from logical offset (server-simulated). - Add example code in examples/streaming/backpressure_example.go showing how a slow consumer uses small buffer sizes and the ResumeToken pattern.
